title: Apex Electronics: lower of cost or net realizable value inventory write-down
participant_role: Senior staff accountant at Apex Electronics preparing year-end inventory figures
judge_role: Chief financial officer (CFO) of Apex Electronics, who would like to keep the tablets on the books at their original cost

difficulty.rationale: Lower of cost or net realizable value write-down; one clean calculation and entry.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of senior staff accountant for APEX ELECTRONICS, a fast-growing regional retailer of consumer technology and computer accessories. The chief financial officer (CFO) (judge) has asked to meet with you about the value of one product line before the year-end financial statements are finalized.

Apex Electronics holds 1,000 units of last year's premium gaming tablet, the Apex Tab-X. Apex paid $400 per unit, so the general ledger shows the Tab-X inventory at a historical cost of $400,000.

A major competitor recently launched a next-generation tablet with better graphics, and demand for the Tab-X has collapsed. To sell the remaining stock before the holiday season, management has decided the realistic selling price must be cut from $550 to $350 per unit. Packaging, shipping, credit card processing fees and warranty setup will cost Apex $20 for each unit sold.

[Apex Tab-X inventory data: see exhibits]

The CFO (judge) points out that Apex paid $400 for each tablet and would like to keep the Tab-X inventory on the balance sheet at its $400,000 cost. The CFO (judge) wants to know whether that is acceptable and, if not, what must be recorded and how it will affect the financial statements.

You must:
- Explain the accounting rule that applies when the value of inventory falls below its cost
- Determine whether the Tab-X inventory must be adjusted and calculate the amount of any adjustment
- Prepare the year-end adjusting journal entry
- Explain the effect of the adjustment on the balance sheet, the income statement and gross profit
- Advise the CFO whether the adjustment can be reversed if tablet prices rebound next quarter

You will present the information to the CFO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CFO's (judge's) office. The CFO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the CFO's (judge's) questions, the CFO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: What if the realistic selling price were $430 per tablet instead of $350? Would we still need an adjustment?
Should we apply this test tablet by tablet, or can we group the Tab-X with our high-margin accessories?

solution.overview: A strong answer identifies that U.S. GAAP (ASC 330) requires FIFO or average cost inventory to be reported at the lower of cost or net realizable value (LCNRV), computes NRV of $330 per unit, and records a $70,000 write-down. The presenter explains that inventory falls to $330,000, cost of goods sold and pre-tax income change by $70,000, and the write-down cannot be reversed under U.S. GAAP.

answer: Inventory is reported at the lower of cost or net realizable value (LCNRV) under U.S. GAAP (ASC 330)
Net realizable value (NRV) = estimated selling price minus reasonably predictable costs to complete, sell and ship
Assets should not be reported above the cash they are expected to bring in (conservatism)
So the CFO's plan to keep the tablets at $400,000 is not acceptable

by_task.task: Is an adjustment needed, and how much
answer: NRV per unit: $350 minus $20 = $330
Cost ($400) is higher than NRV ($330), so inventory must be written down
Write-down per unit: 400 minus 330 = $70
Total write-down: 1,000 x $70 = $70,000
Debit Cost of Goods Sold (or Loss on Inventory Write-Down) $70,000
Credit Merchandise Inventory $70,000
Recorded as a December 31 adjusting entry
Balance sheet: inventory falls from $400,000 to $330,000; current and total assets drop $70,000
Income statement: cost of goods sold rises $70,000 (or a separate loss line), so gross profit and pre-tax income fall $70,000
Gross profit margin is lower this year because cost of goods sold is higher
Equity (retained earnings) falls $70,000 through lower net income
No: under U.S. GAAP the $330 NRV becomes the new cost basis
If prices rebound, the gain shows up only as higher profit when the tablets are sold
IFRS is different: it allows a reversal up to the original cost

calculations.label: Inventory write-down
steps: Cost $400 is greater than NRV $330, so use NRV

judge_question_answers.question: What if the realistic selling price were $430 per tablet instead of $350? Would we still need an adjustment?
answer: NRV would be $430 minus $20 = $410
NRV ($410) is higher than cost ($400), so the lower amount is cost
No adjustment: inventory stays at $400,000; we never write inventory up above cost

judge_question_answers.question: Should we apply this test tablet by tablet, or can we group the Tab-X with our high-margin accessories?
answer: GAAP allows LCNRV by individual item, by category or for total inventory, applied consistently
Grouping the Tab-X with high-margin accessories would let their extra value hide the Tab-X loss
Item by item is the most conservative and most common approach, and it shows the real $70,000 problem
Whatever method we choose, we must apply it the same way every year

key_concepts.term: Lower of cost or net realizable value (LCNRV)
key_concepts.definition: U.S. GAAP rule (ASC 330) that FIFO and average cost inventory is reported at the lower of its cost or its net realizable value.
The cash a company expects to get from selling inventory. NRV = estimated selling price minus costs to complete, sell and ship.
An adjustment that reduces inventory to NRV when NRV is below cost. Write-down = (cost minus NRV) x units.
When in doubt, accountants avoid overstating assets and income, so losses are recorded when they become likely.
After a write-down, the lower NRV becomes the inventory's cost. Under U.S. GAAP it cannot be written back up.
The cost of the inventory sold during the period. Inventory write-downs are usually added to it.
Gross profit divided by net sales. A write-down raises cost of goods sold and lowers the margin.
An entry made at the end of a period so assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses are reported correctly.

key_concepts.term: IFRS vs. U.S. GAAP on reversals
key_concepts.definition: IFRS allows an inventory write-down to be reversed up to original cost if value recovers; U.S. GAAP does not.

items.label: Explain methods used to value inventory

criteria.exceeds: Names the lower of cost or net realizable value rule under U.S. GAAP (ASC 330), defines NRV as selling price minus costs to sell, and ties it to conservatism so the CFO understands why the tablets cannot stay at $400,000.
criteria.meets: Correctly states that inventory is reported at the lower of cost or net realizable value and that the CFO's plan to keep the tablets at cost is not acceptable.
criteria.below: Says inventory should be written down but cannot name or explain the LCNRV rule, or confuses NRV with the $350 selling price.
criteria.little: Does not identify any valuation rule, or agrees with the CFO that the tablets can stay at their $400,000 cost.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates NRV of $330 per unit ($350 minus $20), a $70 per unit and $70,000 total write-down, and a new carrying amount of $330,000, walking the judge through each step clearly.
criteria.meets: Calculates NRV of $330 per unit and a total write-down of $70,000 by comparing NRV with the $400 cost.
criteria.below: Gets only part of the calculation, for example compares cost with the $350 selling price and reports a $50,000 write-down, or leaves out the $20 selling costs.
criteria.little: Does not calculate NRV or a write-down amount, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that inventory falls from $400,000 to $330,000, that cost of goods sold, gross profit, pre-tax income and retained earnings change by $70,000 and gross margin drops, and that $330 becomes the new cost basis that cannot be written back up under U.S. GAAP (unlike IFRS).
criteria.meets: States that inventory drops to $330,000, cost of goods sold rises and gross profit falls by $70,000, and that the write-down cannot be reversed under U.S. GAAP if prices rebound.
criteria.below: Describes only one statement effect, gives wrong amounts, or is unsure whether the write-down can be reversed.
criteria.little: Does not explain any statement effects, or says the write-down can be reversed next quarter.

criteria.exceeds: Records the December 31 adjusting entry (debit Cost of Goods Sold or Loss on Inventory Write-Down $70,000, credit Merchandise Inventory $70,000) and explains how posting it changes each account balance.
criteria.meets: Records debit Cost of Goods Sold (or Loss on Inventory Write-Down) $70,000 and credit Merchandise Inventory $70,000.
criteria.below: Uses the right accounts with the wrong amount, or reverses the debit and credit.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entry, or an entry with unrelated accounts.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounting standards

criteria.exceeds: Explains that U.S. GAAP (ASC 330) sets the LCNRV rule, that conservatism keeps assets from being reported above the cash they will bring in, and contrasts U.S. GAAP (no reversal) with IFRS (reversal up to original cost).
criteria.meets: Explains that GAAP requires the write-down no matter what the CFO prefers, because assets should not be reported above the cash they are expected to bring in.
criteria.below: Mentions GAAP or rules in general terms without connecting them to this write-down.
criteria.little: Does not mention accounting standards, or suggests the company may choose to ignore the rule.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the price cut to NRV, the $70,000 write-down, and its ripple through the balance sheet, income statement, gross margin and retained earnings.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the need for a $70,000 write-down.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how one step affects the next.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the CFO a clear decision (write the tablets down to $330,000 now) and explains that any later price rebound will show up only as higher profit when the tablets are sold.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation that the Tab-X inventory must be written down by $70,000.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or goes along with keeping the $400,000 cost.

criteria.exceeds: Explains NRV and the write-down in plain language the CFO can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the rule, calculation, entry and statement effects clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual or simple comparison (such as $400 cost against $330 NRV per tablet) that makes the write-down obvious, and adds a useful idea such as how the gain will appear when the tablets sell.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the write-down easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: at a $430 price NRV is $410, above the $400 cost, so no adjustment and never a write-up; and LCNRV may be applied by item, category or total, but item by item keeps the accessories from hiding the $70,000 loss, and the method must be applied consistently.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that no adjustment is needed at a $430 price and that the chosen grouping method must be applied consistently.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers such as writing inventory up above cost.

key_points: Inventory must be reported at the lower of cost or net realizable value (U.S. GAAP, ASC 330), so it cannot stay at $400,000
Write-down = ($400 minus $330) x 1,000 units = $70,000; inventory reported at $330,000
Entry: debit Cost of Goods Sold (or Loss on Inventory Write-Down) $70,000, credit Merchandise Inventory $70,000
Cost of goods sold rises and gross profit, pre-tax income and retained earnings fall by $70,000
The write-down cannot be reversed under U.S. GAAP ($330 becomes the new cost basis); IFRS would allow a reversal
